Abstract
Purpose  Lung cancer is a life-threatening disease that poses a significant risk to human health. Accurate 
differentiation between benign and malignant lung nodules, based on computed tomography (CT), is crucial to 
assess lung health. Developing an automated computer-aided diagnostic method for this differentiation is essential. 
We introduced a streamlined 3D model structure to solve the problems of 2D models cannot extract spatial 
information effectively and 3D models have high complexity and large occupation of computing resources.
Methods  We proposed an MSA (multiple self-attention-based) model to address the limitations of 2D models 
in extracting spatial information effectively and the high complexity associated with 3D models. Our approach 
introduced the 3D RTConvBlock, which employed multiple self-attention mechanisms for the extraction of spatial 
features. This enabled the extraction of specific spatial feature information by combining local features, global 
information, and dependencies between features.
Results  The MSA model demonstrates exceptional performance with an accuracy of 0.953, a sensitivity of 0.963, and 
an AUC (area under curve) of 0.993 in the LUNA16 dataset, which is higher than state-of-the-art methods. Compared 
with existing 2D models, we extract spatial information features better, resulting in higher accuracy.
Conclusion  These results have significant implications for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of lung nodule 
classification, providing robust auxiliary support for physicians diagnosing lung diseases.
Keywords  Image processing, Lung nodule classification, Residual convolution, Self-attention mechanism

Given the varying shapes and complexities of lung nod­
ules, coupled with the shared visual attributes of benign 
and malignant nodules observable in diagnostic criteria, 
the task of distinguishing between benign and malignant 
nodules poses a significant challenge, even for experi­
enced radiologists [5, 6]. This difficulty is amplified when 
radiologists review CT images one by one [7, 8], attempt­
ing to ascertain the malignancy probability based on the 
information presented in the images. Hence, the primary 
task is the differentiation of benign from malignant lung 
nodules during the screening process using CT images.
At present, the analysis of benign and malignant lung 
nodules based on their morphological manifestations in 
CT images presents a significant challenge. Identifying 
nodule type often relies on the radiologist’s experience, 
so it needs more objectivity and consistency [9]. Further­
more, the vast quantity of a patient’s CT images makes 
the diagnostic process both time-consuming and labor-
intensive. Due to high workload intensity and potentially 
poor image quality, manual reading can sometimes lead 
to misjudgments in nodule diagnosis.
As depicted in Fig. 1, benign and malignant lung nod­
ules exhibit noticeable differences in shape and size. A 
clear distinction between benign and malignant nodules 
can be made with the naked eye when viewing the 3D 
images of lung nodules extracted from the lung paren­
chyma. However, lung nodules are inherently complex, 
typically surrounded by background tissue, with lesions 
potentially occurring anywhere within the lungs. Directly 
visualizing extracted lung nodules amidst background 
tissues, such as lung parenchyma, is not feasible in a 
clinical setting. Therefore, developing a CAD method 
for automatic nodule differentiation between benign and 
malignant nodules is essential.
Aiming at the problem that the existing 3D mod­
els have high complexity and the fine-grained features 
of nodules are difficult to extract, we propose a more 
streamlined model integrated the advantages of residual 
convolutions and attention mechanisms to improve the 
overall classification performance and reduce the com­
plexity of the model.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
1.	 To effectively extract the spatial fine-grained features, 
we designed a high-performance lung nodules 
classification network integrated the multiple 
multihead self-attention mechanisms to enhance the 
ability of feature extraction.
2.	 We propose a method called RTConvBlock that first 
extracts local and edge information and then fuses 
global features, effectively extracting spatial feature 
information at different scales.
3.	 In order to reduce the number of model parameters, 
we propose a novel model, which introduces 
concatenated residual convolution to effectively 
reduce the number of model parameters.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Sec­
tion 2 provides an over-view of related work. Section 3 
details our proposed method. In Section  4, we present 
our results along with comparative experiment data. 
Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper.
Related work
Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems, employ­
ing single or multiple algorithms, are efficient tools for 
enhancing the quality of health diagnoses [10]. Tradi­
tional CAD systems primarily focus on extracting hand-
crafted features from lung nodules to train models for 
automated nodule classification. This methodology uti­
lizes various feature sets to train classification algorithms, 
including support vector machines [11], linear discrimi­
nant analysis [12], and random forests [13]. While this 
method yields satisfactory results for well-defined nod­
ules, it needs to exhibit more efficacy in classifying nod­
ules of diverse shapes and sizes, particularly in images 
with blurred backgrounds. In recent years, the rapid 
advancement of deep learning, specifically in the domain 
of natural image processing, has stimulated an increasing 
number of researchers to adopt deep learning techniques 
for medical image processing [14–16]. Consequently, 
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged 
as a potent alternative for nodule classification tasks.
Regarding 2D methodologies, Al-Shabi et al. [17] pro­
posed a Local-Global network that employs 3 × 3 kernel

size residual blocks for local feature extraction and nonlo­
cal blocks for global feature extraction. This approach 
analyzes nodule density and structure for local features 
and nodule shape and size for global features, achieving a 
classification accuracy of 0.926. Xie et al. [18] introduced 
a multiview knowledge-based collaborative deep model 
to extract features from different nodule views, learning 
about edge and texture information. While their model 
achieved an accuracy of 0.961 in classifying benign and 
malignant lung nodules, it exhibited high computational 
complexity. Huang et al. [19] employed a classification 
method that fused a deep transfer CNN with an extreme 
learning machine to extract high-level nodule features, 
improving nodule diagnosis results with an accuracy of 
0.946. Zhai et al. [20] utilized a multitask CNN method 
to learn 3D nodule features from nine 2D views, thereby 
preserving subtle nodule features, although different 
views were not necessarily related. Shi et al. [21] intro­
duced a transfer learning strategy to optimally use labeled 
and unlabeled data for nodule classification, achieving an 
accuracy of 88.3% on their private dataset. However, their 
sample of benign and malignant nodules was imbalanced.
3D methods have also been applied to classify benign 
and malignant lung nodules. Shen et al. [22] proposed 
a multiconvolutional neural network, termed 3D multi­
crop CNN, which employs a multiscale downsampling 
method for automatically extracting nodule protrusion 
information. While it achieved an accuracy of 0.871, the 
approach lacked automatic nodule detection. Lv et al. 
[23] introduced a segmented, extracted, and classified 
convolution network, incorporating a multilayer percep­
tron for nodule classification and using gradient descent 
to mitigate gradient dispersion. This method achieved a 
classification accuracy of 0.960. Li et al. [24] combined 
manual features with learned features from the output 
layer of 3D CNNs as input to a support vector machine. 
They optimized feature subsets using sequential for­
ward feature selection methods, reaching an accuracy 
of 0.886, despite an unbalanced sample. Zhang et al. 
[25] constructed a deterministic annotation dataset with 
confirmed pathological labels, proposing a collaborative 
learning framework to facilitate deterministic nodule 
classification by integrating knowledge from uncertain 
annotation data through nodule segmentation and malig­
nant scoring regression. Despite data imbalance, this 
approach achieved a classification accuracy of 0.917. Xie 
et al. [26] proposed the SSAC model, based on CNN, 
which used adversarial training to minimize the discrep­
ancy between the input nodules and the reconstructed 
ones, achieving an AUC (Area Under Curve) of 0.958, 
accuracy of 0.925, and sensitivity of 0.849, despite an 
imbalance in labeled and unlabeled samples. Zhang et al. 
[27] integrated the benefits of SENet and ResNeXt, dem­
onstrating its ability to enhance feature discriminability, 
achieving an accuracy of 0.917 and an AUC of 0.956. The 
MSCS-DeepLN model proposed by Xu et al. [28], which 
employed the 3D CNN as the backbone, combined three 
models, and used multiscale input cropped from CT 
images. This network could learn multilevel contextual 
features while preserving diversity, achieving an AUC of 
0.940, accuracy of 0.926, sensitivity of 0.855, and F1-score 
of 0.879, albeit with limited data. Liu et al. [29] proposed 
a multimodel approach to extract advanced features, 
effectively improving generalization ability and obtain­
ing an AUC of 0.939, accuracy of 0.906, and sensitivity of 
0.837. Xia et al. [30] proposed an attentive network with 
residual and squeeze-and-extraction attention to extract­
ing spatial and contextual features, achieving an accuracy 
of 0.919 and an F1-score of 0.910, although the model 
demonstrated high complexity.
Our proposed MSA method offers a novel approach by 
restructuring the traditional Transformer architecture, 
we decompose the multi-layer Transformer encoder and 
reconnect the components with residual connections, 
creating a more efficient framework for 3D nodule analy­
sis. This architectural innovation allows parallel attention 
heads to simultaneously capture diverse spatial rela­
tionships within lung nodule volumes while maintain­
ing computational efficiency. This attention approach is 
particularly valuable for lung nodule classification where 
both fine-grained internal features and broader con­
textual information are diagnostically significant. Fur­
thermore, our implementation integrates MSA within a 
computationally efficient framework that reduces param­
eter count compared to previous 3D models while main­
taining superior performance, alleviating the parameter 
inefficiency issues in earlier approaches like those by Xia 
et al. [30] and Zhang et al. [25]
In summary, the 2D model falls short in extracting the 
spatial information of lung nodules, while existing 3D 
models, due to their large volume, numerous parameters, 
and complex algorithms, entail high computational costs. 
To address this issue, we propose a more streamlined 
algorithm which reduces the number of computations. 
Additionally, the interference from background tissue 
poses a significant challenge to the task of benign versus 
malignant classification. To counter this complex back­
ground tissue interference, we have embedded a multi­
head self-attention mechanism into the proposed model 
that captures contextual information from various levels.
Experiment and results
The software environment was implemented on the 
Linux operating system, utilizing 4 NVIDIA TitanXP 
GPUs as the hardware environment. The programming 
and development environment was facilitated through 
CUDA Toolkit 10.0. Furthermore, the programming lan­
guage employed was Python 3.8, and the deep learning

framework used was PyTorch. For the learning process, 
the Adam optimizer was utilized. Additionally, due to 
the GPU memory limit of 12 GB, the batch size was con­
strained to 8. Training of the learning model was per­
formed over 100 epochs with a learning rate set at 0.0001. 
The Cross-Entropy Loss Function [31] served as the loss 
function in our approach.
Evaluation metrics
To provide a comprehensive evaluation of our model’s 
classification performance under various training strat­
egies, we calculated several indicators, including accu­
racy, precision, sensitivity, F1 score, and the Receiver 
Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve. In this context, 
NT P  denotes the number of samples correctly identified 
as positive by the model; NF P  is the count of negative 
samples incorrectly categorized as positive; NT Nsignifies 
the number of negative samples correctly identified; and 
NF N stands for the number of positive samples misclas­
sified as negative.

Ablation experiment
This study conducted a comparative analysis of train­
ing and evaluation for different network variations. As 
depicted in Fig.  2, we devised distinct models for pul­
monary nodule classification. The VGG network struc­
ture serves as the baseline model. ResVGG denotes the 
addition of residual connections to the baseline. ResV­
VGG signifies the incorporation of a vision transformer 
encoder into the ResVGG model.
We adopted VGG as the baseline model. Table 1 pres­
ents a comparative analysis of the effects of the addition 
of different components on classification performance. 
According to Table 1, The ResVGG model with residual 
connections demonstrates superior performance com­
pared to the baseline VGG because residual structures 
create alternative pathways for gradient flow during back­
propagation, effectively addressing the vanishing gradient 
problem. This architectural improvement enables more 
effective feature propagation and representation learn­
ing, particularly important for capturing subtle nodule 
characteristics. While this design introduces additional 
parameters (49.9 M vs. 32.9 M), the substantial improve­
ments in accuracy (1.2%) and sensitivity (3.1%) justify 
this increase. Notably, despite the parameter increase, 
the FLOPs actually decrease slightly (19.4B vs. 20.1B) due 
to more efficient feature utilization through the residual 
pathways Based on ResVGG, the sensitivity of the model 
is improved by introducing ViT. This is because the self-
attention mechanism in ViT can better weight the fea­
tures at different locations, so as to capture the global 
features more accurately and improve the sensitivity 
of the model to malignant nodules. However, the large 
size of ViT leads to an increase in the number of model 
parameters and FLPOs.
As shown in Table 1, our proposed model achieved an 
accuracy of 0.953, a sensitivity of 0.963, and an F1 score of

For our lung nodule classification task, we selected 
the 4-layer configuration after careful consideration of 
the complexity-performance trade-off. While deeper 
networks (8 or 12 layers) have the theoretical capacity 
to learn more complex features, they also significantly 
increase computational demands and the risk of overfit­
ting, especially given our dataset size. The 4-layer model 
achieved strong performance metrics (accuracy of 0.953 
and sensitivity of 0.963) while maintaining reasonable 
computational requirements. This configuration pro­
vides sufficient depth to capture the relevant features for 
nodule classification while ensuring efficient training and 
inference times.
Table 3 demonstrates the effect of different numbers 
of attention heads (2, 3, and 4) on model performance. 
Increasing the number of heads from 2 to 4 leads to con­
sistent improvements across all performance metrics, 
with accuracy rising from 0.936 to 0.953 and sensitivity 
from 0.945 to 0.963. The ROC curve, as shown in Fig. 
6, further illustrates these performance improvements. 
This improvement occurs because multiple attention 
heads allow the model to focus on different aspects of 
the nodule features simultaneously, capturing more com­
prehensive spatial relationships. The AUC value reaches 
0.993 with both 3 and 4 heads, but the 4-head configura­
tion yields better results in other critical metrics. While 
increasing the number of heads does increase computa­
tional demands slightly (FLOPs increase from 57.19B to 
57.77B), this modest 1% increase in computational cost 
yields significant performance gains. Our experiments 
showed that using more attention heads would result in 
diminishing returns relative to the increasing computa­
tional costs, making 4 attention heads the optimal con­
figuration for our lung nodule classification task.

by comparing it with other classification methods based 
on pulmonary nodules. Table  4 presents a comparison 
with these methods, focusing on lung nodule classifica­

an SSTL-DA 3D CNN network to eliminate the super­
fluous noise from input samples, achieving an accuracy

of 0.911 and an AUC of 0.958. However, their method 
was computationally intensive. Wu et al. [36] proposed 
a coarse-to-fine self-supervised network, STLF-VA, to 
resolve the interference from diverse background tissues, 
achieving an AUC of 0.972 and an accuracy of 0.924. 
Nevertheless, the large number of parameters resulted 
in a significant computational load. But our model com­
pared with those of SSTL-DA [35] and STLF-VA [36], 
is more computationally efficient. Accuracy has been 
increased by up to 42%. Guo et al. [3] fused asymmet­
ric and gradient enhancement mechanisms to maximize 
the spatial information utilization of nodules and effec­
tively extract more refined multiscale spatial information, 
achieving a classification accuracy of 95.18%. Nonethe­
less, their approach had issues related to sample size 
disparities. Our approach demonstrates superior perfor­
mance compared to Nodule-CLIP [37] due to fundamen­
tal differences in the feature extraction methodology. The 
Nodule-CLIP model relies on U-Net segmentation as a 
preprocessing step, which inevitably introduces segmen­
tation errors that propagate through the classification 
pipeline. In contrast, our method employs manual nodule 
extraction, circumventing these segmentation-induced 
errors.
However, according to the sensitivity index analysis, 
our model does not fare as well as SAACNet [3], possibly 
due to their added adjustment factors of the loss function 
that increase focus on challenging and misclassified sam­
ples, a feature our loss function lacks. But our method 
boasts an accuracy of 0.953, marginally surpassing them 
with an accuracy of 0.952.
In summary, the model we propose exhibits excellent 
performance in classifying benign and malignant lung 
nodules. Given the heterogeneity of pulmonary nodules, 
3D models like ours capture more comprehensive spa­
tial information and extract representative features more 
effectively than their 2D counterparts. Furthermore, our 
model not only optimizes the deep network effectively 
but also extracts valuable feature information, thereby 
enhancing classification performance.
Conclusion
In this study, we introduced a model for distinguishing 
between benign and malignant pulmonary nodules. Our 
model combined ConvBlock, which designed concat­
enated residual convolution, and RTConvBlock, which 
incorporated concatenated residual blocks and multiple 
multihead self-attention mechanisms. This unique amal­
gamation enabled the extraction of image features at 
various levels and scales, thereby enhancing the feature 
extraction capabilities of the model. Experimental results 
verified the superior performance of the model in the 
classification task of pulmonary nodules.
Despite achieving promising results, our developed 
method has certain limitations that warrant further 
consideration. First, in the context of hand-crafted fea­
ture-based CADx systems, the extraction and selection 
of features is a complex and time-consuming process. 
Moreover, these performance of the system can be incon­
sistent when evaluated across different databases due to 
their sensitivity to minor changes in nodule types. Thus, 
the necessity for high-quality lung nodule datasets is 
increasingly evident. Second, our current method relies 
solely on manually extracted features for nodule extrac­
tion, without incorporating a nodule segmentation sys­
tem, thereby lacking automation. Consequently, future 
work should concentrate on enhancing the quality and 
quantity of datasets, addressing the issue of insufficient 
labeled samples, and improving automated performance.
Method
Our work consists of 3 major stages: (1) dataset acqui­
sition; (2) nodule extraction; (3) training our proposed 
method for nodule classification. A summary of the pro­
posed method is shown in Fig. 7.
Data acquisition
The dataset utilized in this study is the LUNA16 data­
set (Lung Nodule Analysis 2016) [38], derived from the 
LIDC-IDRI (Lung Image Dataset Consortium and Image

CT images with slice thicknesses greater than 3 cannot

As the LUNA16 dataset does not contain benign and 
malignant labels, we have derived nodule labels from the 
LIDC-IDRI dataset. We adopt the benign and malignant 
evaluation rules provided by the LIDC-IDRI dataset, 
where the malignancy score of the nodule ranges from 1 
to 5 (minimum 1 point, maximum 5 points).
To assure the dependability of labels, following a rig­
orous labeling method in Al-Shabi et al. [40], only these 
lung nodules that were marked by at least 3 radiologists 
are sampled to ensure the consistent evaluation of the 
presence of nodules. Specifically, nodules with an aver­
age malignancy score equal to or near 3 were excluded, 
where malignancy or benignity could not be determined. 
Nodules with an average malignancy score above 3 were 
labeled as malignant, while those with lower scores were 
labeled as benign. After this screening process, 497 nod­
ules were selected for the study. There are 239 benign 
nodules and 258 malignant nodules. Finally, we divide the 
nodule data into training and test datasets according to 
8:2 to verify the nodule classification performance of the 
system.
Nodule extraction
Before training the data, it is essential to perform pre­
processing steps for nodule extraction. Initially, the data 
is resampled to a uniform resolution, and areas of water 
and air are filtered using the threshold method. Subse­
quently, the data range is truncated to −1000-600HU, and 
the processed image is normalized to a range of 0–255. 
The distribution of the selected nodule sizes is detailed in 
Table 5. Upon completion of the original preprocessing 
of the images, we commence the extraction of the nodule 
based on the center of the nodule.
The central coordinates and pixel intervals of the origi­

dinates of the nodule, as provided in the csv file under

Model
In this paper, we propose an end-to-end network archi­
tecture for lung nodule classification. As depicted in 
Fig.  8, our model consists of a ConvBlock and three 
RTConvBlocks. Our model contains two convolutional 
structures, ConvBlock and RTConvblock, which focus 
on different feature information. Considering the over­
all complexity of the model, we use RTConvblock in the 
middle three layers, focusing on the key features and 
contextual information of the image. This structure effec­
tively reduces the computational complexity of the model 
and improves the model performance and effect. Our

The RTConvblock module is a structure that contains 
a ConvBlock and a Transformer Encoder [42]. Among 
them, ConvBlock is used for local feature extraction, 
while the Transformer encoder is responsible for global 
context modeling. The Transformer encoder in the mod­
ule contains 4 attention heads (num_head = 4) and 4 lay­
ers of stacking (num_layer = 4). The multihead attention 
mechanism can adaptively pay attention to different 
spatial positions and feature subspaces, thereby provid­
ing richer feature correlation capabilities. The number of 
stacked layers allows the RTConvblock module to convey 
and integrate context information more deeply, further 
improving the feature expression ability.
The Transformer Encoder module implements the 
Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture. It begins with a 
patch embedding step, where the input tensor is divided 
into patches and linearly projected to obtain patch 
embeddings. The position embeddings, representing the 
spatial information of each patch, are then added to the 
patch embeddings. The resulting embeddings undergo 
dropout for regularization and are passed through the 
transformer encoder, which consists of multiple mul­
tihead self-attention. These transformer layers enable 
capturing global dependencies and modeling long-range 
interactions between patches. Finally, the output embed­
dings are reshaped and passed through a 1 × 1 × 1 convo­
lutional layer to generate the final output.

Abstract: Purpose Lung cancer is a life-threatening disease that poses a significant risk to human health. Accurate differentiation between benign and malignant lung nodules, based on computed tomography (CT), is crucial to assess lung health. Developing an automated computer-aided diagnostic method for this differentiation is essential. We introduced a streamlined 3D model structure to solve the problems of 2D models cannot extract spatial information effectively and 3D models have high complexity and large occupation of computing resources. Methods We proposed an MSA (multiple self-attention-based) model to address the limitations of 2D models in extracting spatial information effectively and the high complexity associated with 3D models. Our approach introduced the 3D RTConvBlock, which employed multiple self-attention mechanisms for the extraction of spatial features. This enabled the extraction of specific spatial feature information by combining local features, global information, and dependencies between features. Results The MSA model demonstrates exceptional performance with an accuracy of 0.953, a sensitivity of 0.963, and an AUC (area under curve) of 0.993 in the LUNA16 dataset, which is higher than state-of-the-art methods. Compared with existing 2D models, we extract spatial information features better, resulting in higher accuracy. Conclusion These results have significant implications for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of lung nodule classification, providing robust auxiliary support for physicians diagnosing lung diseases.
